This was the first such reduction in four years and was larger than some economists expected. The entities agreed to pay combined civil penalties of $392.75 million, were censured, and ordered to cease and desist from future violations. This enforcement action was part of an ongoing SEC sweep targeting such violations, which have resulted in billions of dollars in fines since 2021. Notably, three firms received significantly reduced penalties for self-reporting their misconduct. [6, 7, 9, 12] The CMS Innovation Center's goal to have all Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030 is also a major catalyst. [1, 3] This transition incentivizes providers to focus on the quality and effectiveness of care over the quantity of services, utilizing alternative payment structures like bundled payments and shared savings contracts. [2, 4] Consequently, there is an increased emphasis on preventive care, managing social determinants of health (SDoH), and leveraging technology and data analytics to improve patient outcomes and control costs. [5, 7] PE firms are also targeting healthcare information technology to enhance efficiency, as providers and payers grapple with margin pressures and regulatory changes. This deal value marks a 39% increase from the previous quarter's $28.2 billion and a 405% surge compared to the second quarter of 2023. The volume of deals also rose, showing a 29% increase from the prior quarter and a 13% rise year-over-year. The largest deal in the sector during this period was the $9.2 billion investment in Vantage Data Centers Management by DigitalBridge Group and Silver Lake Technology Management. <8> In the second quarter of 2024, global private equity fundraising experienced a decline, with $150.8 billion raised, marking an 11% decrease from the first quarter's $168.8 billion. The slowdown was also reflected in the number of funds reaching a final closing, which fell to 184, a 2.6% drop from the 189 funds that closed in the previous quarter. A separate report from Preqin noted similar trends, calculating that $151.5 billion was raised by 177 funds in Q2 2024. This report highlighted a regional divergence, with North America-focused funds raising $105.4 billion, a 24% increase, while Europe-focused funds saw a 63% decrease to $28.7 billion.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In the fourth quarter of 2024, M&A activity in the Human Capital Management (HCM) sector saw a notable increase, continuing a rebound that began in the first half of the year after a slowdown in late 2023. [2, 3, 6] This trend indicates a potential industry expansion period, with some reports noting over 440 total acquisitions in 2024, a 23% increase from the previous year. [2, 4] A key driver for this activity is the growing interest from insurance brokers and accounting firms, such as Arthur J. Gallagher, One Digital, EY, and Smith+Howard, which are acquiring HCM capabilities to broaden their service offerings. [3, 6] Additionally, a surge in demand for outsourcing services like HR, payroll, and IT, driven by the rise of remote and flexible work models, contributed significantly to the M&A volume. [2] <2> A Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz report published on January 24, 2025, noted that 2024 developments in Delaware caselaw could make it more difficult for private equity sponsors to use the MFW framework to shield deals from litigation. A key development was the Delaware Supreme Court's ruling in *In re Match Group, Inc. Derivative Litigation* on April 4, 2024. This decision clarified that for the MFW framework to apply, all members of a special committee must be independent, not just a majority. The court also affirmed that entire fairness is the presumptive standard of review for any transaction where a controlling stockholder receives a non-ratable benefit, unless both prongs of the MFW framework—an independent committee and a majority-of-the-minority stockholder vote—are met from the outset. <3> A market analysis from the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, published in late January 2025, expressed quiet optimism for a breakout year in private equity deal activity. The report highlights that improving market valuations, alongside robust credit and equity capital markets, are creating a more favorable environment for both new deals and exits. The analysis suggests that the combination of record-high levels of deployable capital and a growing need for sponsors to secure liquidity events will likely lead to an increase in private equity dealmaking in 2025. A Q3 2024 EY survey indicated 53% of General Partners expect an increase in exits, and multiple sources confirm that exit activity and sentiment improved throughout late 2024. <4> The outlook for the private equity (PE) market in the first quarter of 2025 indicates a period of recovery and innovation, though perspectives on the strength of this recovery vary. A US-led rebound is anticipated, bolstered by economic resilience and adjustments in interest rates. A key driver of activity is expected to be technology-focused growth, with significant investments anticipated in AI, SaaS, and digital infrastructure. Improved financing conditions are also predicted to stimulate a rise in middle-market deals. The secondary market is another area expected to see continued growth, providing liquidity options for investors. <5> A report from S&P Global Market Intelligence published on December 12, 2024, indicates that private equity and venture capital investment in the U.S. solar industry was poised to hit a four-year low in 2024. Through November 26, 2024, private equity inflows into the U.S. solar sector amounted to $3.1 billion, a 24.6% decrease from 2023 totals. This decline in the U.S. contrasts with a global rebound in private investment in the solar sector, which saw a deal value of $25.04 billion in 2024, a 52% increase from the previous year. The majority of this global investment was directed towards Europe, which attracted over $20 billion across 23 deals. <6> A report from Heidrick & Struggles, published on December 11, 2024, indicates that compensation for North American private equity investment professionals saw modest gains in 2024, contrary to prior expectations that it would flatline. The survey, which compiled data from 820 professionals, found that 62% of respondents reported an increase in base salary between 2023 and 2024. There was also a slight increase in the percentage of professionals who received larger bonuses for 2023 compared to the previous year. Furthermore, the report highlighted an increase in the use of clawbacks and holdbacks at the managing partner level. <7> A consensus among financial analysts suggests that private equity dealmaking will increase in 2025, rebounding from a multi-year slowdown. This optimistic forecast is attributed to several key factors, including near-record levels of deployable capital, often referred to as 'dry powder'. Additionally, there is mounting pressure on private equity sponsors to generate liquidity and return capital to their limited partners (LPs) after several years of extended holding periods. The anticipated recovery is also supported by improving macroeconomic conditions, such as economic resilience, expected interest rate adjustments, and more favorable credit markets. While the overall outlook is positive, Despite these challenges, the significant amount of capital waiting to be deployed and the large number of companies held in portfolios for extended periods are expected to drive activity. <8> According to a report from S&P Global Market Intelligence, the combined private equity and venture capital deal value in the U.S. and Canada reached $30.92 billion in October 2024. This amount is nearly double the value from the same period in 2023. While deal value rose, the number of deals declined by approximately 5.8% year-over-year, falling to 1,042 from 1,106. Globally, the total private equity and venture capital transaction value for October 2024 was $63.28 billion, a 65.8% increase from October 2023. <9> A final rule from the U.S. Department of the Treasury, issued on October 28, 2024, became effective on January 2, 2025. This rule implements Executive Order 14105, which President Biden issued on August 9, 2023, to address national security threats posed by 'countries of concern' developing sensitive technologies. The rule restricts or requires notification for U.S. investments in entities within the People's Republic of China, including Hong Kong and Macau, that are involved in semiconductors and microelectronics, quantum information technologies, and specific artificial intelligence applications. The regulations apply to various transaction types, including equity investments, certain debt financing, and some limited partner (LP) investments, affecting a broad range of U.S. persons and the foreign entities they control. <10> On October 18, 2024, Armanino LLP, a top 25 U.S. accounting and advisory firm, finalized a deal for a strategic minority investment from private equity firm Further Global Capital Management. [2] The transaction, which also closed on this date, was notable as Armanino became the largest U.S. accounting firm to sell a minority stake while retaining both operational and ownership control. [2, 4] This investment is intended to accelerate the firm's growth in technology, particularly in AI, fuel its merger and acquisition strategy, and aid in talent retention. [4] Following the investment, Armanino will reorganize into an alternative practice structure, with Armanino CPA LLP handling attest services and Armanino Advisory LLC providing all other consulting and tax services. [3]

Consequently, while deal value in the first half of 2025 was up from the previous year, Q2 saw a slowdown, and exit activity and fundraising have struggled to keep pace. In a direct response to this executive order, the DOL on August 12, 2025, rescinded its December 2021 supplemental statement. The 2021 guidance had discouraged plan fiduciaries from including private equity as an investment option, suggesting they often lack the necessary expertise to evaluate such complex investments. The rescission of this guidance marks a significant policy shift, aiming to reduce regulatory burdens and litigation risks for fiduciaries, and to provide American workers with greater access to a wider range of investment opportunities, including private equity, real estate, and digital assets, within their defined contribution retirement plans. <3> Dallas-based private equity firm Trive Capital announced a series of promotions that were effective July 1, 2025. In a news release on August 7, 2025, the firm recognized Tanner Cope, Andrew Frank, Joe McDougall, and Brad Wiginton on their promotions to Partner. The announcement also included heartfelt congratulations for 17 other team members on their respective promotions. Trive Capital, which manages over $8 billion in regulatory assets, noted the promotions reflect exceptional performance and meaningful contributions to the firm's culture. <4> Private equity faces significant challenges in its efforts to penetrate the $12 trillion U.S. 401(k) market. [1, 5, 7] Historically, plan fiduciaries have been cautious, citing concerns over high fees, the illiquid nature of the assets, and potential fiduciary risks, which has limited adoption despite a 2020 Department of Labor (DOL) information letter that permitted their inclusion. [3, 4, 7, 11] On August 7, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to encourage the inclusion of alternative assets, including private equity and cryptocurrency, in these retirement plans. [1, 2, 5] The order directs the DOL and other regulators to clarify guidance on fiduciary responsibilities for plan sponsors offering these more complex investments. [7, 8] While investment firms lauded the move, critics and some experts point to the heightened risks for retirement savers. [2, 9] Widespread adoption is not expected to be immediate, as it will take time for regulations to be written and for employers to revise their plans. [2] <5> On August 7, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at facilitating the inclusion of alternative assets, such as private equity, real estate, and cryptocurrencies, into 401(k) and other defined-contribution retirement plans. [1, 2, 3] The order directs the Department of Labor to reexamine and clarify its guidance regarding fiduciary duties under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) when offering funds containing these assets. [3, 7, 8] It also mandates consultation with the Treasury Department, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and other federal regulators to align regulations and encourage the adoption of these investments. [4, 5, 8] This move could potentially unlock a significant pool of capital, estimated at over $12 trillion, for the alternative asset management industry. [2, 5] While supporters, including investment firms, lauded the order for providing workers with more investment options and the potential for higher returns, some analysts expressed concern over the risks associated with investing retirement funds in speculative and less-regulated assets like cryptocurrency. [1, 2] <6> Private equity firm Carlyle Group announced strong second-quarter 2025 results on August 6, 2025, for the quarter ending June 30, 2025. The firm reported a record $323 million in fee-related earnings, an 18% increase year-over-year. Assets under management (AUM) also reached a new high of $465 billion. During the quarter, Carlyle raised $13.4 billion in new capital, with performance driven by its private credit and secondaries platforms. In conjunction with the results, the Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.35 per common share. <7> Frazier Healthcare Partners has finalized the sale of its portfolio company, Elevate Patient Financial Solutions, a provider of technology-enabled revenue cycle management (RCM) services. The buyers are Audax Private Equity and Parthenon Capital, who have made a strategic investment to support Elevate's future growth and acquisitions. [2, 6, 7] Frazier acquired Elevate in 2019, when it was known as MedData, and fostered its growth through investments in talent, technology, and seven strategic add-on acquisitions. [2, 3] The sale was officially announced on August 4, 2025, through press releases from the involved parties. [2, 6, 9, 10] The transaction itself closed on July 31, 2025. [6] <8> The Women's Private Equity Summit is scheduled to take place from March 8-11, 2026, at the Arizona Biltmore in Phoenix, Arizona. This annual event brings together an anticipated 1,200 women professionals from the private equity industry for networking, discussions, and deal-making. The summit is designed to foster authentic connections through a variety of activities including morning hikes, fireside chats, dynamic panels, and networking receptions, offering over 24 hours of content and 25 hours of networking opportunities. It aims to create a uniquely welcoming environment for leaders who value openness, inclusivity, and high-impact conversations. <9> On July 31, 2025, the global law firm K&L Gates announced the appointment of 14 partners to new practice area leadership roles. [1, 2, 5] This move is part of a broader strategic leadership transformation aimed at empowering the firm's next generation of management. [4, 5] The appointments followed other recent leadership changes, including Stacy Ackermann becoming the new Global Managing Partner on July 1, 2025. [1, 7] Several of the new leaders were appointed to practices highly relevant to private equity, including Clair Pagnano (Lead Practice Area Leader, Asset Management and Investment Funds), Sasha Burstein (Practice Area Leader, Asset Management and Investment Funds), Ed Dartley (Practice Area Leader, Asset Management and Investment Funds), Adam Tejeda (Lead Practice Area Leader, Corporate), Adam Kelson (Practice Area Leader, Corporate), and Jessica Pearlman (Practice Area Leader, Corporate). [1, 2]

The combined entity operates across 14 states with 77 ambulatory infusion centers, providing comprehensive specialty care across immunology, neurology, gastroenterology, rheumatology, ophthalmology, and other complex disease states. <3> Shore Capital Partners has announced the merger of its portfolio companies, Reliant Healthcare and Care Fusion Rx. The merger aims to establish a nationwide infusion therapy platform by combining complementary strengths to expand access to comprehensive home and ambulatory infusion center services. <4> New York-based middle-market private equity firm Argand Partners was honored with the M&A Deal of the Year award ($50-$100 million) at the 24th Annual M&A Advisor Awards for its acquisition of the global dancewear brand Capezio. <5> Private investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) announced a definitive agreement to acquire the US packaging giant Sealed Air in an all-cash, take-private transaction valued at approximately $10.3 billion. <6> A Juniper Square analysis of the PitchBook Q3 2025 US PE Breakdown report indicates that a Federal Reserve interest rate cut in September helped to revive investor confidence and increase private equity deal activity. The report, published on October 23, 2025, noted that year-to-date deal and exit values for 2025 had already surpassed 2024 totals. Despite these positive trends in deals and exits, fundraising continued to lag. The Federal Reserve announced a quarter-point rate cut on September 17, 2025, bringing the federal funds rate to a range of 4% to 4.25%. This was the first interest rate reduction since December 2024. <7> In its "Q3 2025 US PE Breakdown" report, PitchBook revealed a notable surge in US private equity activity. Deal value saw a significant quarter-over-quarter increase of 28% and a 38% rise year-over-year, with the total deal value for the year already surpassing that of 2024. Technology transactions were a primary driver of this growth. The report also highlighted a 22.4% quarterly increase in exit counts, the first significant spike since 2021. PitchBook analysts suggest this indicates that "more assets are beginning to move through the system." <8> Ares Management announced the final closing of its Ares Secondaries Infrastructure Solutions III (ASIS III) fund, securing approximately $3.3 billion in equity commitments. This amount significantly surpassed its initial $2 billion target after the fund hit its hard cap. The fund is more than three times the size of its 2021 predecessor, making the total capital raised one of the largest infrastructure secondaries campaigns to date. This successful fundraising highlights a growing trend and increased demand for liquidity solutions within the dynamic private infrastructure secondaries market. The ASIS III fund aims to invest in a diversified portfolio of established private infrastructure assets using flexible secondary solutions, such as GP-led continuation vehicles and traditional Limited Partner interest acquisitions. <9> In the third quarter of 2025, U.S. private equity investment surged to a 14-quarter high of $300.1 billion, according to KPMG's "Pulse of Private Equity" Q3 2025 report. This significant increase in deal value was primarily driven by a handful of large take-private transactions. Notable megadeals for the quarter included the acquisition of gaming company Electronic Arts for approximately $55 billion by a consortium including Silver Lake, Affinity Partners, and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the purchase of aircraft leasing company Air Lease for $28.2 billion by investors including SMBC Aviation Capital and Sumitomo Corporation, and the acquisition of HR software firm Dayforce by Thoma Bravo for $12.4 billion. This report, which covers the quarterly period ending September 30, 2025, was first announced via a KPMG press release on October 1, 2025. <10> On August 25, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit remanded two SEC rules aimed at increasing transparency in short-selling and securities lending back to the agency for further consideration. The court found that the SEC had acted arbitrarily and capriciously by failing to properly assess the combined economic impact of the two rules, which were adopted on the same day in October 2023. The rules, Rule 10c-1a (Reporting of Securities Loans) and Rule 13f-2 (Short Position and Short Activity Reporting), were challenged by several industry associations. While the court upheld the SEC's statutory authority and the notice-and-comment process for the rules, it sided with the petitioners on the issue of the cumulative economic analysis. This decision creates uncertainty for these regulations, which impact the trading strategies of private funds and investment managers. The SEC must now re-evaluate the economic consequences of the rules, and it is anticipated that any revised rulemaking may be narrower in scope.
